stanzas: Rosa das rosas e Fror das frores,
Dona das donas, Sennor das sennores.
Rosa de beldad' e de parecer
e Fror d'alegria e de prazer,
Dona en mui piadosa seer,
Sennor en toller coitas e doores.
Rosa das rosas e Fror das frores...
Atal Sennor dev' ome muit' amar,
que de todo mal o pode guardar;
e pode-ll' os peccados perdõar,
que faz no mundo per maos sabores.
Rosa das rosas e Fror das frores...
Devemo-la muit' amar e servir,
ca punna de nos guardar de falir;
des i dos erros nos faz repentir,
que nos fazemos come pecadores.
Rosa das rosas e Fror das frores...
Esta dona que tenno por Sennor
e de que quero seer trobador,
se eu per ren poss' aver seu amor,
dou ao demo os outros amores.
Rosa das rosas e Fror das frores...
orig.credit: Cantigas de Santa Maria (court of Alfonso X, 1252–1284): Cantiga 10, Rosa das rosas

stanzas: Rose of roses and Flower of flowers,
Lady of ladies, Lord of lords.
Rose of beauty and of fair appearance
and Flower of joy and of delight,
Lady in being most merciful,
Lord in taking away sorrows and pains.
Rose of roses and Flower of flowers...
Such a Lord a man must greatly love,
who can guard him from all evil;
and can pardon him the sins
that he commits in the world through evil desires.
Rose of roses and Flower of flowers...
We must greatly love and serve her,
for she strives to keep us from going astray;
and also makes us repent of the wrongs
that we commit as sinners.
Rose of roses and Flower of flowers...
This lady whom I hold as Lord
and whose troubadour I wish to be,
if I can by any means have her love,
I give the other loves to the devil.
Rose of roses and Flower of flowers...

notes: line 1.2 and throughout: 'Sennor' (later 'senhor') is the form the troubadour lyric uses for the beloved lady, as her feudal lord; it is kept as 'Lord' because the song sets 'Dona' (Lady) and 'Sennor' side by side. 'Lady of ladies, Lady of lords' is a possible reading of the second half.
line 2.3-4: literally 'Lady in being very merciful, / Lord in removing griefs and pains'; 'coitas' are sorrows, troubles or the pains of love.
line 3.4: 'per maos sabores' is literally 'through bad tastes': evil appetites, sinful pleasures.
line 4.2: 'punna' is 'strives, makes an effort'; 'falir' is to fail, err or fall into sin.
line 5.3: 'per ren' is 'by any thing, by any means'.
The repeated refrain line ('Rosa das rosas e Fror das frores...') stands for the whole two-line refrain in the source; it is translated as it stands, with its dots.
